why: The semicolon terminates a statement.

q: Which of these causes undefined behaviour?
options: Adding two unsigned ints that wrap around
why: Out-of-bounds access is undefined behaviour; unsigned wrap-around is well-defined.

title: Add two numbers
statement: Read two integers and print their sum.
io:
Input: two integers a and b separated by a space.
Output: a + b.
hint: Use cin >> a >> b to read both numbers. Use long long for big values.

title: Even or odd
statement: Read an integer and print Even or Odd.
io:
Input: one integer n.
Output: the word Even or the word Odd.
hint: n % 2 == 0 means even. Note that -3 % 2 is -1 in C++, not 1, so test for == 0.

title: Largest of three
statement: Read three integers and print the largest.
io:
Input: three integers separated by spaces.
Output: the largest one.
hint: Keep a variable for the best value so far and compare it with each number.

title: Reverse a line
statement: Read a whole line of text and print it reversed.
io:
Input: one line of text (may contain spaces).
Output: the same line written backwards.
hint: cin >> stops at spaces — use getline(cin, s) to read the full line.

title: Count vowels
statement: Read a line and print how many vowels it has.
io:
Input: one line of text.
Output: the number of vowels (a, e, i, o, u in either case).
hint: Loop over every character and use tolower() so you only compare with five letters.

title: Factorial
statement: Read n (0 ≤ n ≤ 20) and print n!.
io:
Input: one integer n.
Output: n factorial. Remember 0! = 1.
hint: 20! does not fit in an int — use long long.

title: Count the primes
statement: Read n and print how many prime numbers are ≤ n.
io:
Input: one integer n (1 ≤ n ≤ 1000000).
Output: the count of primes up to and including n.
hint: Trial division for each number is too slow for 1,000,000. Use the Sieve of Eratosthenes.

title: Nth Fibonacci
statement: Print the nth Fibonacci number (F0 = 0, F1 = 1).
io:
Input: one integer n (0 ≤ n ≤ 90).
Output: F(n).
hint: Keep only the last two values in a loop. F(90) needs long long.

title: Balanced brackets
statement: Check whether a string of brackets ()[]{} is balanced.
io:
Input: one line made of the characters ( ) [ ] { }.
Output: YES if every bracket is closed in the right order, otherwise NO.
hint: Use a stack: push opening brackets, and when you see a closing one it must match the top of the stack.
